content: The relative benefits of surgical intervention for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) are highly dependent on the specific subgroups of patients targeted. A systematic review and meta-analysis conducted in 2016 could not clearly identify which types of patients would benefit most from surgery or which surgical interventions would yield the greatest benefit. The expected effect of surgery is moderate for the average patient deemed suitable for such an intervention. However, this finding may be biased, as patients undergoing surgery often have other factors predisposing them to poor outcomes, which cannot always be adjusted for in analyses. Programs with limited access to surgical facilities may prioritize patients who remain sputum smear-positive, have resistance to multiple drugs, and exhibit localized pulmonary disease. Preoperative evaluations may include computerized tomography (CT), pulmonary function testing, and quantitative lung perfusion or ventilation studies. Surgical resection should be timed to maximize the likelihood of cure while minimizing harm, ideally when the disease is localized to one lung or a single lobe. At least two months of medical therapy should precede surgery to reduce bacterial infection in surrounding lung tissue. Prognosis improves when partial lung resection is performed after culture conversion. Even with successful surgery, the total duration of treatment and post-culture conversion therapy should follow established guidelines. Partial lung resection for MDR/RR-TB patients should only be considered in facilities with well-trained and experienced thoracic surgeons and stringent infection control measures. Inadequate surgical facilities or untrained personnel may increase morbidity and mortality. Infection control during surgery is critical due to the generation of infectious aerosols and materials. Postoperative pulmonary hygiene and mechanical ventilation are also essential. Direct laboratory testing of resected lung lesions can provide valuable information, and treatment regimens may need adjustment based on these findings. The role of surgery in MDR-TB treatment remains uncertain due to the lack of high-quality evidence. Observational data from case series, which formed the basis of the 2016 recommendations, may be biased. For example, no patients with HIV or extensive disease in the dataset had undergone surgery. Additionally, there is insufficient data on adverse events, surgical complications, or long-term sequelae to allow meaningful analysis. Conversely, the effectiveness of surgery may have been underestimated due to the absence of appropriate control groups. Corticosteroids have been used as adjunctive therapy for severe TB complications, such as miliary TB, respiratory failure, central nervous system involvement, and pericarditis. The 2017 WHO guidelines recommend initial corticosteroid therapy with dexamethasone or prednisolone tapered over 6–8 weeks for patients with tuberculous meningitis (strong recommendation, moderate certainty). For tuberculous pericarditis, corticosteroid therapy may be used (conditional recommendation, very low certainty). These recommendations are limited to these two forms of extrapulmonary TB. Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) shows that corticosteroids reduce mortality, severe disability, and relapse in TB meningitis, with greater benefits in more severe cases. Adverse events, including severe hepatitis, were lower in patients receiving steroids. For TB pericarditis, steroids showed benefits in reducing mortality, constrictive pericarditis, and improving treatment adherence. While these recommendations primarily apply to non-MDR-TB, they may also be relevant for MDR/RR-TB patients receiving effective TB treatment regimens. However, corticosteroids should only be used when clearly indicated, as they are immunosuppressive and can weaken the body’s ability to fight TB if used inappropriately. Immunomodulators have been explored as potential adjuncts to MDR-TB treatment, aiming to shorten treatment duration and enhance immunity to prevent recurrence. However, no candidate agents have demonstrated efficacy, and further research is needed to develop effective immunotherapy agents. A Phase I trial in Belarus reported higher treatment success in MDR/XDR-TB patients receiving autologous bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cell infusions alongside chemotherapy, with no serious adverse events observed. These findings warrant further trials to assess this therapeutic approach. The role of interferon-gamma, a cytokine essential for antimycobacterial host defenses, remains unclear. A review of its use as adjunctive therapy found no RCTs, and the only randomized, placebo-controlled trial was halted prematurely due to deaths in the experimental arm. The lack of high-quality evidence precludes the recommendation of interferon-gamma as part of MDR/XDR-TB regimens under programmatic conditions. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended for all HIV-infected patients with drug-resistant TB requiring second-line anti-TB drugs, regardless of CD4 cell count, and should be initiated as early as possible, ideally within the first 8 weeks of starting anti-TB treatment (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Delaying ART increases the risk of mortality in HIV-infected TB patients. ART should be initiated in all TB patients living with HIV, including children, regardless of CD4 count or clinical stage, within 8 weeks of starting anti-TB treatment. Potential drug-drug interactions and overlapping toxicities between antiretrovirals and TB drugs should be managed, but these rarely necessitate modifications to MDR-TB or ART regimens. Close monitoring for response and toxicity is advised for patients on both treatments. Patient-centered approaches are essential to maximize treatment adherence and enable early detection of non-responders. Communityor home-based directly observed therapy (DOT) is conditionally recommended over health facility-based DOT or unsupervised treatment. Video-observed therapy (VOT) can replace DOT where technology is available and appropriately organized. Additional interventions, such as food or financial support, psychological counseling, home visits, and use of information technology, can promote adherence. These interventions should be tailored to individual patient needs and available resources. Programmatic implementation of MDR-TB regimens requires revising policy and operational documents, training staff, and ensuring patient support. Electronic recording and reporting systems should be introduced or improved to standardize data collection on drug susceptibility testing, prescribed treatments, outcomes, and adverse reactions. Such data are critical for future evidence-based recommendations and global policy-making.
